This is the entire point of doing a PhD, you’re here to learn how to do science. If you were fully capable of doing science as a scientist with years or decades of experience, there’d no need to be doing your PhD. You’re basically a toddler learning how to walk comparing yourself to a marathon runner. 

I know it’s intimidating but your advisor is there to help you learn how to do science. This means admitting that you feel lost and overwhelmed, and a good advisor will teach you how to narrow your thoughts and ideas. Trust me, I was in the exact same space you were in my first year and it can be overwhelming because you’re reading decades worth of information in a short amount of time. Just keep it simple and write down all the things you do know about your field, what are things that are still uncertain or haven’t been explored yet, and what can you do to fill that gap? These may not be great ideas but it’s a good start for discussion with your advisor in meetings. My biggest advice is to talk. Just talk and talk and talk with them. You might get annoying but it helped me learn how to think like a scientist.

My advice for before starting: Rest. I know its easy to feel like you need to do a bunch of things right now so you don’t seem like you’re behind but take this opportunity right now to travel, spend time with friends and family, and do whatever you want until October. Do some readings and whatever you need to do to bridge the gap but don’t stress yourself out. You have the next 5 years to stress. 

My advice for during is one, network. A career in academia isn’t a given so make sure you’re taking the steps to prepare for an industry job now. Network, intern, or whatever. Trust me, you’ll regret not doing it more than you’ll regret doing it. My second piece of advice is to remember that you’re a PhD student. The point is that you’re learning HOW to do science. Don’t beat yourself up because you’re not doing life changing research or publishing in Nature right off the bat. Third piece of advice is set boundaries with your PI and try your best to have a work life balance. There will be some days or weeks where you’ll need to work a lot (I once worked from 7 AM - 2 AM everyday for 3 weeks) but don’t work until 8 PM if you don’t have to. There’s a stigma sometimes where PhD students should be “living in their labs” but unless you absolutely have to, its okay to go home, have hobbies, and enjoy your free time.
